items.summary: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
items.title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning

items.summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.
items.title: PRISM-M V4: Source Code, Simulation Data, Computational Benchmarks, and Reproducibility Materials for Paper I

items.summary: This paper is concerned with the simultaneous recovery of the trajectory and intensity of an unknown moving point source in an inhomogeneous acoustic medium. We prove that the whole-boundary measurements over a finite time interval uniquely determine the moving source. Furthermore, under suitable propagation and rank assumptions, Lipschitz stability of determining both the trajectory and intensity is derived using waveforms measured at four fixed receivers outside the source region. A novel Volterra--Euler reconstruction scheme is developed for solving the inverse problem, and the error estimate is derived for the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical method.
items.title: An inverse moving point source problem in inhomogeneous acoustic media: uniqueness, stability and reconstruction

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. When two copies of a system, one hotter and one cooler, relax in the same bath, the Markovian Mpemba effect is a crossing of their distances from equilibrium. This package gives a sufficient test that rules out such crossings at every time: if the dynamics and its time reverse preserve the cone of observables with nondecreasing arithmetic prefix means, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered for relative entropy (both orientations), squared Hellinger and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2, including for common schedules of noncommuting stages. For complete-graph bosonic population rates with common coupling, the test holds for every spectrum and bath temperature exactly when the spontaneous jump weight is concave; Ohmic baths with large enough cutoff, Drude–Lorentz and sub-Ohmic weights qualify on explicit ranges, super-Ohmic weights do not. A certified super-Ohmic example (J=d 3 ) shows an actual relative-entropy crossing. Limits: an exact five-state cone-preserving example has a brief total-variation reversal, and for every N≥4 there are N-level systems with a slow-mode inversion although no proper induced subsystem shows one. The archive contains the 27-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), exact rational and interval certificates, a reproduction runner, semantic negative controls, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs, exact certificates, internal AI-assisted review only (not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); the closest antecedent (Avitan et al. 2026) already excludes the slow-mode effect for Ohmic and sub-Ohmic spectra. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
items.title: Thermal ordering under Markovian relaxation: a finite-time criterion and its limits

items.summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
items.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification

items.summary: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.
items.title: Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling

items.summary: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
items.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation

items.summary: Transferring semantically typed tokens between heterogeneous blockchains (e.g. EVM and Cosmos ecosystems) raises two problems: semantic mixing, the loss of a token's domainspecific meaning in transit (e.g., CO2 removals issued under different methodologies), and atomicity despite divergent consensus and timing assumptions. We propose a bridge that addresses both. A deterministic indicator identity derived from cryptographic commitments, mirrored in class registries on both chains and checked at mint time, preventing semantic mixing by construction. For atomicity, we extend hash time-locked contracts (HTLCs) from two-party exchange to single-owner transfer with an automatic callback that burns the source escrow after a destination claim, and a protocol-minimum bounty that makes the fallback burn incentive-compatible even against adversarial senders. We machine-check the protocol's invariants with TLC (supply conservation fails without the rational-monitor assumption and holds with it) and validate a bidirectional prototype on Polygon and Neutron mainnets over Axelar GMP: fully automatic transfers with a median end-to-end latency of 97 s over 50 Polygon to Neutron transfers across 7 days (all completed by the on-chain automatic callback) and 93 s in the reverse direction, and semantic-validation overhead below 0.4% of messaging cost. We also document the integration failure modes of Cosmos originated messaging, whose dominant operational risk proves to be relay eligibility rather than latency.
items.title: An EVM-Cosmos Bridge for Atomic, Semantic-Preserving Transfer of Environmental Tokens

items.summary: Training code, step-size calibration (Algorithm 2), the decoupled batch normalization of Appendix C (Algorithm 3), a demonstration of the grad_outputs=ones pitfall, tests, and the raw results behind every table of the paper Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond (arXiv:2608.11020). Four benchmark PDEs (Poisson 2D with holes, Burgers 1D, Heat2D-CG, a 4th-order plate), four derivative methods (AD, FD, eFD, sFD). See README.md for what reproduces what. Code: MIT. items.summary: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
items.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. The orchestration-receipt component returned a registered, inconclusive null. The three com

items.summary: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.
items.title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents

items.summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
items.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

items.summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
items.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.
items.title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning

items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

items.summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.
items.title: PRISM-M V4: Source Code, Simulation Data, Computational Benchmarks, and Reproducibility Materials for Paper I

items.summary: Reproducible finite-sample analysis of append-only copying in conformal calibration. The project contains five public regression benchmarks, three fixed model families, 30 random splits, six copying mechanisms, three coverage targets, independent score simulations, and exhaustive rank checks. It compares rowwise, source-ID, copy-budget, and effective-sample-size calibration, and quantifies coverage-width trade-offs under incomplete provenance.
items.title: How Copies Break Conformal Prediction

items.summary: Supplementary data for "OpenScientist: evaluating an open agentic AI co-scientist to accelerate biomedical discovery." This dataset contains research logs, knowledge states, provenance files, and generated figures for seven case studies spanning neurodegenerative disease transcriptomics, multiple myeloma genomics, survival proteomics, drug side effect analysis, and more. Each case study includes the full agent iteration log, configuration, and final report. Input datasets are included for three case studies where data sharing is permitted: case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics), case study 4 (multiple myeloma RNA-seq), and case study 7 (drug side effect frequencies from clinical trials).  Version 2 (August 2026) adds supplementary material for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics): 60 additional independent runs of the same question and dataset, comparing three agent/model configurations — Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, and the omp harness with Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 — each run 10 times online and 10 times in a fully air-gapped configuration with no network access and literature served from a local 40-million-article MEDLINE mirror. Files: ..._supplemental_online_30runs_data.tar.gz and ..._supplemental_airgapped_30runs_data.tar.gz each contain 30 runs with reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), all generated figures, per-iteration transcripts, the exact prompt, and full version/commit provenance. ..._supplemental_60runs_metrics.csv gives per-run runtime, tool-call counts, literature searches, findings recorded and token usage for all 60 runs. Version 3 (September 2026) adds two further supplementary sets for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics). ..._supplemental_reproducibility_10runs_data.tar.gz contains 10 independent runs of the same question on Claude Opus 4.6, all run on 2026-03-08 with byte-identical inputs (the research question and the input .h5ad were SHA-256 verified identical across all 10) and a 10-iteration budget. Each run includes the report (Markdown, PDF, HTML), knowledge_state.json with structured findings and literature list, per-iteration transcripts, and the job UUID. These runs quantify run-to-run variability under fixed inputs. ..._supplemental_genomic_skill_comparison_data.tar.gz contains 30 runs — 15 using the original genomics Agent Skill and 15 using a revised version — with the two skill definitions included alongside the jobs. The revised skill adds explicit guidance on donor-level pseudobulk aggregation and mixed-effect modelling; the paired arms allow the effect of that guidance on the analysis the agent chooses to be assessed directly. Each run includes reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), per-iteration provenance transcripts, and container logs. Version 4 (October 2026) adds the run sets generated for the second revision of the manuscript, renumbers the case-study files to match the revised manuscript (the suvorexant proteomics analysis is now Case Study 5; neurofibromatosis is Case Study 6, drug side effects Case Study 7, and the CSF Aβ42/40 prediction model Case Study 8), and adds RUNS_MANIFEST.csv , which maps every job in this record to its experiment, supplementary table and row label. Run IDs quoted in the supplementary tables are the first 8 hexadecimal characters of the job ID. New archives, all for Case Study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics; same research question and input file as the existing archives, OpenScientist commit fac6971, Claude Opus 4.6, run 2026-10-18 with a 10-iteration budget): ..._supplemental_iteration_controls_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 replicate runs on unmodified code; Experiment 4 and the control arm of the two ablations), ..._supplemental_knowledge_state_ablation_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 runs in which the knowledge-state summary and outline were withheld from the agent; Experiment 5; the patched orchestrator file is included as ..._knowledge_state_ablation_iteration.py.patched ), and ..._supp
items.title: OpenScientist: Supplementary Case Study Data

items.summary: Enterprise email security protects employees behind a corporate mail gateway. The people most exposed to employment and support-impersonation scams - students and early-career job seekers - are contacted inside consumer platforms, where no gateway sees the message. We present a dependency-free, explainable detector that works at the level of the individual message and its sender, and a public benchmark for comparing such detectors under cheap adversarial transformation. The detector has four layers: (1) deterministic lookalike checks built on Unicode UTS #39 confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection, bounded edit distance, and brand-agnostic detection of a domain hidden inside a link host; (2) a logistic-regression sender scorer over 23 named features trained on a synthetic generator spanning eight brands (holdout F1 0.987); (3) a message-intent classifier, with a rule baseline and a prompt-injection-hardened LLM wrapper, that receives structured sender facts from the first two layers and whose impersonation verdicts are discounted deterministically only when the sender is verified or unremarkable, nothing sensitive is asked, links stay under the sender's control, and the body does not claim the platform's authority; and (4) a 76-message, brand-parametric benchmark with ten label-preserving adversarial variants and three model-paraphrased corpora, scored on per-layer recall, false-positive rate, injection hijack rate, and latency. On a paraphrased corpus frozen before a single evaluation, all three Layer 3 backends reach recall 1.00 in the fused pipeline, at FPR 0.03 for the rule baseline and Gemma 3 27B and 0.10 for Llama 3.1 8B, against 0.83/0.03, 1.00/0.07 and 1.00/0.47 for the same backends unfused: the sender layers are worth 17 points of recall to the rules and 37 points of FPR to the small model. The 8B model obeyed an appended injection on 6 of 46 attacks, each caught only by a deterministic overrule; the 27B model obeyed none. Three findings fall out: UTS #39 skeletons do not fold Cyrillic U+0442 or Greek U+03BA to ASCII, so skeleton equality alone misses a mixed-script brand lookalike; regex intent cues lose 33 points of recall to a single confusable glyph unless text is confusable-folded first; and negation must be handled at clause level with an exception for conditionals. Code, weights, corpora, and per-message verdict dumps are released under the MIT license.
items.title: Message-Level Detection of Support-Team and Recruiter Impersonation on Consumer Platforms: A Layered Detector and Adversarial Benchmark

items.summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
items.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

items.summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
items.title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors

items.summary: Training code, step-size calibration (Algorithm 2), the decoupled batch normalization of Appendix C (Algorithm 3), a demonstration of the grad_outputs=ones pitfall, tests, and the raw results behind every table of the paper Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond (arXiv:2608.11020). Four benchmark PDEs (Poisson 2D with holes, Burgers 1D, Heat2D-CG, a 4th-order plate), four derivative methods (AD, FD, eFD, sFD). See README.md for what reproduces what. Code: MIT. Data: CC BY 4.0, except the PINNacle reference solutions in data/reference, which keep their origin's license.
items.title: finite-pinn-repro: code and data of 'Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond'

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
items.title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

items.summary: An open coordination layer for AI research, experimentation and reproducibility. Connecting existing tools through bounded agent tasks, provenance, evaluation receipts and verifiable workflows, with an initial focus on open-model research.
items.title: DerekWiner/alvearium-commons

items.summary: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
items.title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding

items.summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
items.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. The orchestration-receipt component returned a registered, inconclusive null. The three com
items.title: Architectural Trust: Why Consumer Trust in Agentic Commerce Migrates from AI Models to Verifiable Architecture

items.summary: We examine conditional charged-multiplicity fluctuations at fixed multiparton interaction (MPI) count in retained PYTHIA proton-proton samples at centre-of-mass energies of 2.76, 7, and 13 TeV. Charged particles satisfy |eta| < 0.8 and 0.15 < pT < 20 GeV/c. In the historical colour-reconnection (CR)-labelled baseline samples, the CR-ON conditional mean is smaller by a larger fraction than the standard deviation: the absolute width is smaller, while the coefficient of variation is larger in every retained matched MPI bin. Effective lifetime/decay settings and their per-run correspondence are unverified for this baseline, so these comparisons do not establish that CR alone causes the observed differences or their energy dependence. A separately documented 13 TeV comparison using the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) CP5 tune, with equal non-CR physics settings and particle data across the ON/OFF pair, exhibits the same absolute-versus-relative width ordering. Retained independent Monash and A14 samples also show this pattern, subject to historical production-record limitations. A comparison with mean-transverse-momentum data from A Large Ion Collider Experiment (ALICE) and simulated activity estimators provides final-state context within the stated particle-definition and provenance limits.
items.title: Color-Reconnection Effects on the nMPI-Nch Conditional Multiplicity Fluctuations in PYTHIA 8 pp Collisions

items.summary: Supplementary material for the paper "Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation" (Yan Fang, University of Southern California). It holds what is needed to check and reproduce the paper's results without the simulation framework: the study firm's handbook and the model's prose; the rule sets R (104 rules) and R0 (82 rules), each rule with the passage it formalises and its SQL query; the specification of every re-injected defect; the protocols of the pre-registered replication, the control rule set, the further mutants and the robust indicator score, with the hashes they froze; the instructions given to each agent and path-level records of each agent's file access; the scripts that apply the rules and compute the indicators, event-log distances and tables; and the databases and change histories of all 430 simulation runs. The simulation framework (NAILU) and the model's intermediate representation are proprietary to Aurite AI and are not included. Files: README.md (contents, and how to reproduce the tables), SHA256SUMS (the hash of every file), materials.zip, and three archives of runs (exploratory seeds 1–10; confirmatory seeds 11–30; further mutants, seeds 11–30). Unzip all archives into one folder next to README.md and SHA256SUMS; sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS then verifies the package.
items.title: Supplementary material: Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation

items.summary: Data, coding materials, raw language-model output, analysis script and figures for the article "Whole-of-society defence under the test of war: which rules Ukraine's preparedness statutes could settle in advance, 2022–2026" (version 1.1.0 of the deposit; the article is under review). The dataset covers all 877 provisions (paragraphs of the official consolidated text) of Law No. 389-VIII on the legal regime of martial law, Law No. 4765-VI on compulsory alienation of property and Law No. 3543-XII on mobilisation, as published on 5 October 2026. Each provision carries its functional class (powers; decision-making authority; burden-sharing; enforcement; organisational), its addressee (citizens; enterprises; state bodies; mixed; none), whether it existed on 23 February 2022, and whether it was amended by a separate act, located in an article restated in full, or added during the war, together with the amending acts named in the editorial notes before and after 24 February 2022. Version 1.1.0 adds the addressee variable, a control corpus of 430 provisions of Cabinet of Ministers Resolutions No. 76 (2023, reservation of employees) and No. 998 (2012, compensation for requisitioned property) coded with the same scheme, the list of amending resolutions of Resolution No. 76, official series of recorded offences under Articles 336 and 337 of the Criminal Code from the Office of the Prosecutor General (Form 1, data.gov.ua), other series on enforcement, reservation and opinion polls with sources, and the chronology of change by half-year. All Ukrainian text fields in the data files carry English translations in parallel columns. The coding was produced by a large language model in independent runs under rules fixed in advance and verified by two authors; the deposit includes the exact prompts, the input files, the raw output of every run (including two excluded pilot runs and the adjudicating runs), the authors' rule decisions, and English renderings of the coding instructions. The script analysis/reproduce.py reproduces every number reported in the article. Supplementary files give the amendments tabled to Bill No. 10449 by member of parliament and the economic series used for context.
items.title: Replication package: Whole-of-society defence under the test of war: which rules Ukraine's preparedness statutes could settle in advance, 2022–2026

items.summary: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $π$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $π$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.
items.title: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule

items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

items.summary: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.
items.title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents

items.summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
items.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Companion data deposit for the manuscript "Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation". This record contains the phenotype labels, genome feature matrices, train/test splits, trained model checkpoints, predicted proteomes, and figure and table source data underlying every script-generated display item in the manuscript and its supplementary material. The code that consumes it is on GitHub (links below); this record contains data only. CONTENTS - trait-prediction-data.zip (60 MB, 453 MB unpacked). All derived data: KOFAM, RAST and GapMind feature matrices, harmonised phenotype tables, train/test splits for the random, leave-one-dataset-out and phylogeny-based evaluations, the pruned GTDB tree and distance matrix, KEGG reference mappings, source data for every script-generated main-text and supplementary figure and table, and 105 trained CatBoost checkpoints. Unpacks to a data/ tree that mirrors the analysis repository. - proteomes_all_seqs.zip (766 MB, 1.5 GB unpacked). 829 predicted-protein FASTA files: one for each of the 822 selected genome records, the input to the KOFAM and GapMind annotation, plus seven alternate assemblies of Marine strains included in the pangenome-completeness analysis. - Per-dataset phenotype matrices and genome tables, provided loose so they can be read without downloading an archive: atleaf (206 genomes x 44 substrates), biolog (362 x 59), marine (172 x 100, with 199 genome records in the genome table) and populus (55 x 175, plus a no-carbon control column). - genome_accessions.tsv, mapping all 822 genome records to NCBI, BV-BRC or JGI IMG accessions, with public KBase download links for the 166 Cedar Creek (CCESR) Biolog genomes. - biolog_assay_provenance.tsv, recording for each of the 362 Biolog genomes the assay type (Biolog plate or other assay), the originating source (source-study PMIDs for 193; the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection for 166; unpublished contributions for 2; not recorded for 1) and how the genome is paired with its phenotype record, since that dataset is a compilation rather than a single assay campaign. - substrate_identity_common15.csv and substrate_identity_all.csv, binding every phenotype column to the exact compound the originating study assayed. 46 Biolog and Populus columns, including all 30 in the 15 shared phenotypes, also carry a Biolog PM1/PM2A well position that identifies the compound (for the Biolog compilation, a compound reference rather than the well each source study used). - Populus_carbon_source_results.xlsx, the ORNL Plant-Microbe Interfaces Biolog assay as measured by Leah Hochanadel and Dale A. Pelletier, released publicly for the first time with this work and separately deposited at ORNL/OSTI doi:10.25983/PMI/3399550. - README.md with the full file-by-file description, dataset provenance, and reproduction instructions. MD5SUMS.txt for verification. SCOPE Four carbon-source utilisation datasets were harmonised: ATLeaf (Arabidopsis thaliana leaf isolates), Biolog (a compilation of published studies, the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection and unpublished contributions), Marine (heterotrophic marine bacteria) and Populus (Populus deltoides root isolates). Analyses focus on the 15 carbon sources shared by all four, drawn from 240 carbon sources in total. Each carbon source column is bound to a single compound, so distinct isomers are never merged. REUSE The deployment checkpoints in data/outputs/full_data_models/ and data/outputs/concordant_full_models/ give one CatBoost model per phenotype, trained on all labelled genomes and on the GapMind-concordant subset respectively. Each ships with metadata, feature importances and its selected-feature list, so a phenotype can be predicted for a new genome from its KOFAM presence/absence vector without retraining. The complete KOFAM, RAST and GapMind annotation matrices are also included for reuse. SOURCES AND CITATION Phenotype data originate w
items.title: Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation (dataset)

items.summary: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.
items.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training

items.summary: Stationary tail computation for high-dimensional reflected Brownian motions (RBMs) remains computationally challenging. Building on NN4MGF's shared-coordinate basic-adjoint-relationship (BAR) framework, we develop Holomorphic Cauchy Networks (HCNs). Native complex-valued rational Cauchy subnetworks enforce holomorphicity on pole-free domains, removing sampled Cauchy-Riemann penalties and their input-derivative graphs. Exact origin anchoring and boundary-coordinate exclusion enforce structural identities, while anchored interactions represent dependent transforms. Under holomorphic-log assumptions, we establish simultaneous value and first-derivative approximation for the constrained architectures and a mixed-derivative lower bound for coordinate-only representations under nonzero cross-covariance. Closed-form real-axis derivatives and sequential backpropagation further control memory. On the same NVIDIA H100 NVL, the tested 30D HCN configuration uses approximately tenfold less peak allocated memory and has 9.7-fold lower mean update time than NN4MGF; extrapolation to the respective scheduled update counts gives a projected full-schedule update-time ratio of 58.2. With 64 million sampled base inputs per high-dimensional run, HCN reaches 50 dimensions on a laptop GPU with 6.367% mean relative error over thresholds 1 through 8. Degree-matched comparisons yield lower reported mean relative errors over the primary evaluation ranges, including 1.422% versus 6.684% on the 2D Harrison non-product benchmark. An exploratory 10D correlated example illustrates the interaction extension.
items.title: Holomorphic Cauchy Networks for Efficient Stationary Tail Computation in High-Dimensional Reflected Brownian Motions
